title: BBC in talks with YouTube to produce shows, sell ads abroad, keep licence-fee
excerpt: The BBC is negotiating with YouTube to produce bespoke short- and long-form shows for its YouTube channels, also available on iPlayer and BBC Sounds, targeting younger viewers (BBC Three-style), children’s programming and sports, and could sell advertising on programs shown outside the UK while retaining the licence-fee model domestically.
summary: The BBC is in talks with YouTube to produce bespoke short- and long-form shows for its YouTube channels rather than simply uploading broadcast programs. Those shows would also be available on BBC iPlayer and BBC Sounds. The planned content would target younger viewers, chiefly BBC Three-style shows, children’s programming and sports. Under the proposed arrangement, the BBC could sell advertising on programs shown outside the UK while continuing to rely on the licence-fee model domestically.

title: Warns algorithmic personalized pricing may raise costs for vulnerable Canadians and obscure price signals
excerpt: Vass Bednar highlights the threat posed by algorithmic, personalized pricing, which he asserts leads to price discrimination and obscures price understanding, potentially raising costs for vulnerable households. He stresses the need for transparency and consumer rights regarding these practices, warning that without safeguards, this trend could fragment the market and undermine collective consumer interests.
summary: Vass Bednar argues that Canadians’ affordability pressures increasingly stem from algorithmic, personalized pricing—beyond tariffs or general inflation—where companies tailor prices to individuals’ data, enabling price discrimination. He warns that this personalization can obscure a shared understanding of prices, complicate indicators like the Consumer Price Index, and may raise costs for vulnerable and low-income households, including for essential goods and services. Bednar criticizes the lack of transparency around these practices and calls for greater accountability, including a consumer right to know when personalized pricing is used and, if necessary, legislative action. He cautions that, without such safeguards, the shift toward individualized pricing risks fragmenting the market and treating consumers as isolated individuals rather than part of a collective system.

title: Looksmaxxing reflects a moral crisis that prizes appearance over connection
excerpt: Thomas Chatterton Williams critiques the looksmaxxing movement as a manifestation of a moral crisis among young men, characterizing it as a narcissistic ideology that prioritizes superficial beauty over genuine connection and responsibility, and underscores the potential for self-destructive consequences.
summary: Thomas Chatterton Williams argues that the looksmaxxing movement reflects a moral crisis among young men, describing it as a narcissistic and often cruel ideology with elements of racism and social Darwinism, fixated on extreme and sometimes harmful efforts to enhance appearance. He links this fixation to social fragmentation and broader insecurities, portraying a nihilistic outlook that prizes beauty and status over connection and responsibility. Williams highlights callous, anti-social behavior celebrated within the community and notes a tension between this superficial pursuit and simultaneous gestures toward traditional values. He warns that elevating physical attractiveness as a path to status risks self-destructive outcomes, drawing parallels to literary figures like Dorian Gray.

title: Opinion: Author some travelers are choosing immersive reading retreats over beach vacations
excerpt: The rising trend of immersive reading retreats over traditional beach vacations reflects a desire for deeper engagement with literature and local culture, as noted by Lyn Margerison, who emphasizes the importance of building connections and rekindling enthusiasm for reading through these literary holidays.
summary: The author argues that more travelers are choosing immersive reading retreats over beach vacations, highlighting organized literary holidays that blend deep reading with local culture and community. The author presents Lyn Margerison’s view that these trips ideally mix travel and literature, build like‑minded connections, and rekindle enthusiasm for reading and exploring new places.

title: Exploring Cities Through Endurance Racing
excerpt: Danny Reed, known for racing NYC subways on his bike, advocates for exploration and spontaneity in the city, encouraging everyone to discover the unexpected.
summary:
Danny Reed, the viral sensation behind the daring bicycle races against New York City subways, wants to inspire New Yorkers to embrace adventure in their daily lives. Reed's unique challenges, which involve handing AirTags to subway conductors and attempting to beat the train to its final stop, have captivated online audiences and fellow city dwellers alike.

In an interview with The New York Groove, Reed revealed his passion for exploring the city’s vast terrain, which began when he moved to NYC for college. "I started exploring the city more via bike because it's a great way to do it," Reed shared.

His unconventional races began with the A train, known as NYC's longest subway route. Reed's friendly encounters with transit staff add a social element to his endeavors. "It's fun to talk to the people that are driving these trains every day and don’t get a lot of engagement," he noted.

While Reed's win-loss record stands at five wins to four losses, the spirit of his activities lies beyond competition. He encourages others to explore New York's hidden gems, from beaches accessible by subway to upstate mountain biking trails.

Reed's message is simple yet profound: "Get on your bike and explore. The city's a big place, and every time you get out and go do something, you find something interesting that you weren't expecting."

As Reed continues his races and shares them on social media, he remains a passionate advocate for stepping outside, moving, and letting the city surprise you.

title: RFK Jr.'s 'War on Protein' Is Political Messaging, Not a Nutritional Concern
excerpt: Sam Eagan contends that RFK Jr.'s concept of a ''war on protein'' is a fabricated narrative rooted in political and cultural tactics, emphasizing that most Americans already consume adequate to excess protein and that the prevalent focus on high-protein diets is more about cultural symbolism and marketing than valid health concerns.
summary: Sam Eagan argues that the supposed “war on protein” invoked by RFK Jr. does not exist, framing it as a political and cultural tactic aligned with Trump-era appeals to traditional masculinity rather than a health-based concern. Eagan points to evidence that Americans already consume high levels of protein and cites experts who say many people exceed their needs. He suggests the recent emphasis on animal protein and high-protein diets is driven more by cultural symbolism, marketing, and political posturing than by genuine dietary guidance.

title: Mamdani' cultural references signal his governing identity and public outreach
excerpt: Matthew Schnipper highlights Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s use of cultural references as a significant aspect of his governing style that reflects his identity and mission, engaging diverse constituencies while also raising bold issues like street redesign that have faced opposition.
summary: Matthew Schnipper presents Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s frequent cultural references as a notable feature of his governing style that reflects his identity and vision for the city. He says these nods, delivered at the inauguration and in subsequent appearances, may resonate with different constituencies and help engage the public. Schnipper also highlights Mamdani’s bold stances on issues like street redesign and notes that they have drawn pushback. He plans to track these references over Mamdani’s tenure as a window into his administration.

title: Kathleen Kennedy Discusses Transition at Lucasfilm and Her Return to Producing
excerpt: In an exclusive Deadline interview, Kathleen Kennedy, iconic producer and Lucasfilm president, discusses her transition from leadership to focus on her passion for producing, as she hands over control to Dave Filoni and Lynwen Brennan.
summary:
In a revealing interview with Deadline, Kathleen Kennedy, the esteemed producer and head of Lucasfilm, detailed her plans to step down from her role to return to her first love—producing films. After wrapping up "Star Wars: Starfighter," Kennedy announced she would be passing the leadership baton to Dave Filoni, the Chief Creative Officer, and Lynwen Brennan, the Executive Vice President and General Manager.

Kennedy, who has been instrumental in overseeing the expansion of the Star Wars universe into successful theatrical releases and Disney+ series, explained her decision as a natural evolution. “I want to do more movies,” she expressed, eager to delve back into hands-on filmmaking.

Her tenure involved significant achievements, including overseeing films that grossed $5.9 billion globally and developing critically acclaimed series like "The Mandalorian" and "Andor." Despite the challenges of managing beloved IPs, Kennedy's leadership saw Lucasfilm flourish, engaging new audiences while expanding the Star Wars galaxy into new territories.

Looking ahead, Kennedy aims to embrace new storytelling technologies and collaborate on projects. As she steps back, the future of Lucasfilm under Filoni and Brennan appears robust, with upcoming projects, including a Jon Favreau film due in May, and others from directors like Taika Waititi and Donald Glover.

Kathleen Kennedy's influence remains indelible, and her next chapter promises to be as dynamic as her storied career.

title: Pitti exposes a clash between Italian tailoring and social-media trends, warning economic
excerpt: David Coggins highlights the tension in contemporary menswear between traditional craftsmanship and the influence of social media trends, expressing concern over economic instability impacting small tailoring firms and the lack of clarity in men's dressing standards. He appreciates the artistry of Italian tailors while advocating for a return to simplicity in formal attire.
summary: David Coggins sees contemporary menswear, especially around Pitti, caught between enduring craftsmanship (he cites houses like Liverano & Liverano) and fleeting, social media–driven trends. He describes a lack of consensus about how men should dress; says small European tailoring firms are being hurt by economic instability and trade challenges, leaving American shoppers uncertain about ordering from abroad; and sees the industry clinging to familiar classics rather than pursuing new directions. Coggins praises masterful tonal dressing by skilled Italian tailors, anticipates a rise in bold buffalo plaid tied to traditional outerwear, and advocates simplifying black tie with a straightforward tuxedo. He takes a cautious view of the landscape while acknowledging the enduring elements that continue to shape it.

title: Globes mark a shift from viral spectacle to nuanced, market-aware fashion
excerpt: Robert Williams emphasizes that the Golden Globes red carpet marks a pivotal shift in fashion towards creativity and nuance, prioritizing meaningful design over hyper-viral trends, as brands balance innovation with a cautious approach to image amid a changing market.
summary: Robert Williams says the Golden Globes red carpet signaled a shift toward more creative, nuanced fashion—respecting viewers’ aesthetic intelligence by balancing risk with classicism and avoiding heavy nostalgia—while moving away from gimmicky, hyper-viral looks. He highlights standout appearances by Teyana Taylor and Miley Cyrus and maintains that brands are pushing innovation while carefully managing image in a climate wary of social media stunts. Williams adds that luxury houses appear more selective about visibility and market engagement amid a fluctuating market, and he sees this moment as a turning point toward prioritizing meaningful design over chasing virality.

title: Administration Reopens Whole Milk in Schools, Renewed Debate on Health Impacts
excerpt: Jonel Aleccia highlights President Trump’s signing of the Whole Milk for Healthy Kids Act as a significant shift from previous nutrition standards, with proponents arguing that allowing whole and 2% milk in schools can enhance children’s dietary intake and reduce waste, despite ongoing debates among nutrition experts about the health impacts of full-fat versus lower-fat dairy.
summary: Jonel Aleccia views President Donald Trump’s signing of the Whole Milk for Healthy Kids Act as a notable reversal of Obama-era school nutrition limits, reopening access to whole and 2% milk (alongside nondairy options) for roughly 30 million students in the National School Lunch Program. Aleccia emphasizes supporters’ contention that full‑fat dairy can be a healthy choice, could improve intake by matching children’s taste, and may reduce food waste; Trump also asserts that whole milk is broadly beneficial. She links the move to recent dietary guidelines presented as favoring full‑fat dairy, while underscoring that nutrition experts remain divided over the health implications of whole versus lower‑fat milk and its relationship to childhood obesity.

title: Wikipedia at 25 decentralization replaced gatekeeping and questions need for specialist oversight amid AI
excerpt: Brenda Haas reflects on Wikipedia's 25-year journey from traditional knowledge gatekeeping to a decentralized platform, highlighting tensions around neutrality and ongoing issues like the underrepresentation of women among editors. She contrasts the perspectives of Jimmy Wales, who champions radical openness, with Larry Sanger's belief in the necessity of expert involvement, and raises concerns about the potential impact of AI-generated content on quality and integrity.
summary: Brenda Haas presents Wikipedia’s 25-year evolution as a move from traditional knowledge gatekeeping to a decentralized, collectively edited resource, while emphasizing persistent tensions over neutrality. She contrasts Jimmy Wales’s commitment to radical openness grounded in verifiable sources with Larry Sanger’s view that expert involvement is necessary to mitigate bias. Haas highlights ongoing underrepresentation of women among editors and flags risks that AI-generated content could erode quality. Citing the emergence of Grokipedia, she notes Sanger’s belief that AI could surpass Wikipedia, while Wales remains skeptical of AI-produced entries. Haas cautions that Wikipedia faces continuing challenges to preserve integrity and reliability amid technological change and new competitors.

title: AI's skill at finding software vulnerabilities should prompt a rethink of software
excerpt: Will Knight highlights the growing proficiency of AI in identifying software vulnerabilities, emphasizing that this evolution necessitates a reevaluation of software development and security practices in the tech industry, as it could empower malicious actors while also suggesting the use of AI to bolster defenses and implement secure-by-design methodologies.
summary: Will Knight argues that AI systems are becoming increasingly proficient at finding software vulnerabilities, a development that he and experts he cites say should prompt the tech industry to rethink how software is built and secured. He warns that advancing AI-driven hacking could give malicious actors an edge, and points to responses such as using AI to assist defenders and adopting secure-by-design practices.

title: Autoplay and stripped end credits devalue TV craft and diminish viewer closure
excerpt: Phil Tinline warns that the streaming practice of eliminating end credits through features like autoplay diminishes audience engagement and underappreciates the intricate creative efforts behind television, fostering a culture of instant gratification that can skew expectations for other complex systems. He highlights viewers' increasing demand for weekly releases as a desire for deeper connections to content, emphasizing the need for moments of reflection to help process stories.
summary: Phil Tinline argues that streaming features like autoplay, which minimize or remove end credits, create a subtle shift in audience engagement that undervalues the complex creative work behind television and erodes moments of reflection and closure. He maintains that optimization for retention nurtures instant‑gratification habits that strip context and reduce intricate productions to commodities, a mindset he warns can shape unrealistic expectations for other complex systems, including government. He notes growing pushback—such as viewers’ preference for weekly releases—as a sign of desire for deeper engagement, and he contends that acknowledging endings and credits is essential to help audiences process stories rather than treating entertainment as an endless stream.

title: Analysts suggest global sneaker boom may be cooling
excerpt: Bloomberg News highlights that the global sneaker boom is slowing down, emphasizing that sneaker culture is maturing and brands like Adidas, Nike, and Puma are facing challenges adapting to this shift as the growth that once propelled them is diminishing.
summary: Bloomberg News contends that the long-running global sneaker boom that powered growth at major sportswear companies such as Adidas, Nike, and Puma is showing signs of slowing, citing recent analyst reports; it says sneaker culture is maturing—from markets like Shanghai to resale platforms such as StockX—and that brands are scrambling to adjust as the growth tailwind that drove past gains appears to be waning.

title: Accenture Song is outgrowing the agency model and positioning as a consulting-led marketing orchestration
excerpt: Seb Joseph presents Accenture Song as a transformative force in the marketing industry, evolving beyond traditional agency roles to become a consulting-led entity that integrates advanced technologies and strategic partnerships, ultimately redefining the responsibilities of Chief Marketing Officers towards managing comprehensive growth frameworks. He highlights the urgency of this shift, reflecting concerns that companies lagging in tech adoption risk becoming obsolete.
summary: Seb Joseph presents Accenture Song as having outgrown the agency business without becoming an agency, positioning it “upstream” as a consulting-led control layer that orchestrates the industrial machinery of modern marketing—data architecture, platform integration, workflows, workforce retraining and AI—rather than primarily selling media and creative. He points to Song’s placement within Accenture’s Reinvention Services, its continued expansion via acquisitions, platform investments and deep partnerships with firms like Google, Microsoft, Amazon and Adobe, and its scale (around $20 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue, up about 8% year over year) as evidence that it operates differently from traditional agency holdcos, while noting the revenue comparison to WPP and Publicis is imperfect. As an illustration, he cites Song’s work on a Mondelez generative-AI content platform that is claimed to reduce production costs by 30–50%, coupled with team retraining and redesigned decision systems. In Joseph’s view, this model is reshaping the CMO remit toward owning growth machinery—data pipelines, measurement, martech and workflows—and, once embedded, fosters stickier, structurally dependent relationships; he aligns this with Arthur Sadoun’s observation that clients are increasing spend on consulting and AI projects. Joseph frames this as a potential direction for the marketing business, underscoring urgency with CEO Ndidi Oteh’s emphasis on big-tech partnerships and her warning that “any company that is not a tech company will be irrelevant.”

title: Gordon Sire's "Don't Call It Punk" Ad Reframed Punk as "New Wave" to Broaden
excerpt: Rev. Keith A. Gordon praises Sire Records for its pioneering A&R practices in the late '70s and early '80s but critiques the label's ad campaign that attempted to rebrand punk as ''new wave'' as opportunistic and ironic, noting that the albums promoted are now recognized as punk milestones.
summary: Rev. Keith A. Gordon praises Sire Records for its open‑minded, influential A&R from the late 1970s into the early 1980s—signing underground and groundbreaking artists from CBGB‑era bands like the Ramones, Dead Boys, and Talking Heads to acts such as the Cure, the Smiths, and Madonna (and, in his account, early rap releases by Ice‑T). At the same time, he calls Sire’s 1977 Trouser Press ad headlined “Don’t Call It Punk” tone‑deaf and opportunistic, saying the label aligned with an industry push to rebrand punk as “new wave” to make it more commercially palatable. He acknowledges the ad’s effective layout and copy but deems the attempt to downplay the punk elements futile and ironic, since three of the four featured albums (by Richard Hell & the Voidoids, the Dead Boys, and the Saints, alongside Talking Heads) are, in his view, now regarded as punk milestones.

title: Karten Mosseri misreads AI's impact on Instagram authenticity and urges regulation and creator protections
excerpt: Rachel Karten argues that Adam Mosseri's understanding of AI's impact on Instagram is flawed, as the ''raw'' aesthetic he endorses can easily be mimicked by AI, undermining authenticity and leading to potential erosion of trust among users. She criticizes his proposed solutions as vague and insufficient, advocating instead for concrete measures like regulation and creator protections to effectively address the challenges posed by AI on the platform.
summary: Rachel Karten contends that Adam Mosseri misreads how AI will change Instagram: because the “raw” aesthetic he promotes can be readily simulated by AI, it won’t reliably signal authenticity. She expects creators to differentiate more through craft, ideas, and higher‑effort production rather than deliberate imperfection. Karten warns that the larger risk for Instagram is AI‑driven erosion of trust—users increasingly asking whether posts are AI and feeds filling with low‑quality AI content—which could hurt engagement. She considers Mosseri’s proposed remedies (AI labels, credibility signals, originality ranking, better tools) vague and too passive, and views them as undercut by Instagram’s own AI initiatives. She urges stronger steps, including support for regulation, creator protections and industry standards, and concrete programs to shield creators from AI copycats, instead of framing the challenge mainly as an aesthetic shift.

title: Analysis NHL's suit-code repeal is creating a player-led pregame fashion market
excerpt: Hilary George-Parkin highlights that the NHL’s removal of the suit-and-tie dress code has fostered a new era of player self-expression and fashion opportunities, as evidenced by players collaborating with stylists and brands, while also acknowledging the league's current experimental status compared to others like the NBA.
summary: Hilary George-Parkin (Front Office Sports) says the NHL’s removal of its suit-and-tie requirement has quickly opened space for player self-expression and a nascent fashion economy around pregame tunnel arrivals, creating commercial opportunities that players, teams, agents, and the NHLPA are moving to organize. She describes the shift to dressing “in a manner consistent with contemporary fashion norms” as player-driven and commercially motivated, with the NHLPA’s Steve Scebelo, talent agents, and brand executives citing new partnerships, group-licensing prospects, and growing interest from fashion labels. George-Parkin points to early signals—players working with stylists (examples include Mikhail Sergachev, Auston Matthews, William Nylander, Macklin Celebrini, Connor Bedard), sold-out team collaborations (Anaheim Ducks × Ryoko Rain), social accounts tracking looks, and brand activations (Nylander with Holt Renfrew, Trevor Zegras with Greyson Clothiers, Matthew Schaefer with NoBull)—as evidence the market is responding. She positions the NBA/WNBA tunnel economy as a blueprint while emphasizing hockey remains in an experimental phase and lags those leagues, with the long-term impact still uncertain. George-Parkin also ties the timing to broader attention drivers (the NHL’s return to the Winter Olympics and the TV drama Heated Rivalry) and notes some traditionalist resistance, while maintaining that many players and teams are already testing what resonates.

title: AI-enabled interactivity may alter ebook and audiobook retail models
excerpt: Retailers in the ebook and audiobook market are embracing AI-driven interactive features as a way to enhance user engagement and personalize the reading and listening experience.

title: Creatives should think like creative directors as AI commoditizes execution
excerpt: Alison Weissbrot emphasizes the need for creatives to prioritize human taste over technical execution in an AI-driven environment, warning that while AI can generate numerous polished outputs, it lacks the ability to determine what is meaningful or culturally resonant. She argues that the cultivation of taste, honed through diverse cultural exposure, will become paramount as clients seek agencies that provide judgment and vision rather than mere execution.
summary: Alison Weissbrot contends that in an AI-accelerated creative landscape, taste—human judgment about what truly matters—will be more valuable than technical execution. She says junior creatives will work with AI assistants for art direction and copy, so craft remains useful but is no longer sufficient. She maintains that AI can produce countless polished variations but cannot decide what is meaningful, original, or culturally resonant; without human taste, output risks becoming technically flawless yet homogenous. Weissbrot describes taste as cultivated through broad exposure to culture (art, film, music, niche subcultures), not from models or tools, invoking Rick Rubin’s notion of taste as discerning what feels right, honest, and finished. She expects clients to pay agencies for judgment and vision—whether an idea belongs in culture—more than for execution. Accordingly, she warns creatives to prioritize feeding their cultural inputs and honing taste—studying successful campaigns and reverse‑engineering why they worked—over obsessing about tools, because execution is being democratized while discernment remains scarce.

title: Zucker Netflix' "Members Only" trades on Palm Beach name while largely filmed off-island
excerpt: Andrew Zucker articulates that Netflix’s ''Members Only: Palm Beach'' misrepresents the island by filming primarily in nearby areas and relying on non-authentic portrayals, leading residents to feel that it distorts the community's exclusive identity and contributes to a contentious debate over the true essence of ''Palm Beach.'' He emphasizes local concerns about the series commodifying the area's reputation and suggests that the town's efforts to protect its brand are becoming increasingly challenged by evolving perceptions.
summary: Andrew Zucker says Netflix’s Members Only: Palm Beach trades on the Palm Beach name while mostly filming and setting its story off the island, leaving it, in his view and that of many residents he cites, more label than reality. He points to production permits and on‑screen venues in West Palm Beach and elsewhere as evidence, and relays locals’ complaints that the show feels inauthentic—one likening it to ordering Coca‑Cola and getting Fanta—with some urging the Town to distance itself. Zucker characterizes the series as an outsider take, from its club choices and cast backgrounds to its reliance on flashy reality‑TV tropes, and says residents worry it cheapens or misrepresents the island’s more exclusive, traditional milieu. He also casts the dust‑up as part of a broader tug‑of‑war over who gets to claim “Palm Beach,” noting that nearby businesses and residents seek the cachet while town officials tightly police the brand through measures like chain‑restaurant bans and controlled filming approvals, even as some locals contend the mystique is already widely exposed and evolving.

title: AI is eroding entry-level creative "grunt work" and undermining apprenticeships
excerpt: Nick Geisler contends that the rise of generative AI threatens to eliminate essential entry-level work for aspiring artists, depriving them of valuable mentorship and income opportunities, while also warning that without strong protections, AI could exacerbate inequalities in access to creative careers.
summary: Nick Geisler contends that generative AI is eroding the entry-level “grunt work” that has long served as an apprenticeship for emerging writers, filmmakers, and musicians, and that removing these paid, routine tasks—copywriting, basic editing and first cuts, promotional copy, simple music tracks—shrinks the practice, mentorship, connections, and income that nurture new artists. He points to signals such as estimates of widespread disruption by 2026, studio interest in automation, AI tools like Eddie, and job postings that emphasize training AI over making work as evidence of shrinking opportunities for newcomers. While acknowledging the optimistic view that AI can relieve drudgery, expand capabilities, and democratize tools (and noting his own selective use), Geisler argues that past waves of “digital democratization” mostly enriched large platforms rather than sustaining freelance creatives. He warns that, absent strong safeguards—including mentorship protections sought by groups like the WGA—AI may squeeze livelihoods and undercut the long apprenticeship needed to cultivate artists, concentrating access among the well-connected and nudging culture toward “nepo babies and chatbots.”

title: Thompson Arc Raiders' ML animation benefits gameplay and staff, while its generative TTS raises
excerpt: Tommy Thompson emphasizes that the ethical implications of generative AI in gaming depend on its implementation by studios, arguing that while some uses can enhance player experiences, others, like the generative TTS NPC dialogue in Arc Raiders, diminish quality and harm voice actors' livelihoods. He advocates for ethical experimentation with AI that respects talent and encourages transparent compensation models.
summary:
'- Tommy Thompson distinguishes between Embark’s ML-driven animation in Arc Raiders, which he sees as adding clear player and developer value without displacing animators, and its generative TTS NPC dialogue, which he considers lower-quality and largely a cost-saving move.
- Thompson maintains generative AI is not inherently unethical; the ethics hinge on how studios deploy it and the incentives behind those choices.
- On Arc Raiders’ AI voices, Thompson notes they were reportedly trained on and paid to actors but judges the delivery as lacking emotional weight, timing, and emphasis, offering little player benefit while likely paying performers less than standard rates and setting a harmful precedent for voice actors’ livelihoods.
- Thompson cautions that many AAA studios may adopt generative AI for short-term savings on incidental content, risking perceived quality declines, consumer pushback, and further reliance on AI as revenues tighten.
- Thompson endorses AI uses that demonstrably enhance games and support teams, and he urges ethically and legally sourced experimentation (often by indies), along with compensation models that reflect the value and flexibility AI systems provide.
- To guide purchasing decisions, Thompson offers a checklist: impact on workers’ livelihoods; whether professional talent is being replaced; whether the AI meaningfully enhances quality; and whether the same result could be achieved without generative AI.
- Thompson allows caveats: ethically built voice models and AI-native projects may warrant support, and some actors may want models for convenience or hazardous vocal work; he floats pricing AI voice-model access so actors are comparably compensated and charging a premium for in-studio sessions as a personal proposal.

title: Extra Practice staged pooling can foster convivial support but raises governance and labor trade-offs
excerpt: Extra Practice emphasizes that pooling resources among freelance cultural practitioners can enhance support and improve working conditions, though it also introduces various challenges, such as increased administrative burden and the need for careful coordination. They advocate for experimentation and maintaining a balance between individual practice and collective care, prioritizing structured collaboration to sustain the conviviality essential to creative work.
summary: Extra Practice frames “pooling” for freelance cultural practitioners as a staged process—sharing space, then a name, work, income, and finally mission—that can create convivial support and improve working conditions, while introducing new trade-offs and governance challenges at each step. They say shared studios foster affordable proximity, informal care, and low-barrier collaboration, but require coordination over chores, schedules, and scarce space. A shared name can ease publishing and public programming and attract peers, while raising tensions around authorship, group vibe, and public representation. Sharing work and invoicing can open opportunities and legitimacy but increases administrative labor, role frictions, and burnout risk. Pooling income may offer material security (such as steadier pay and pensions) yet demands trust, protocols, and negotiation, and can provoke guilt, fears of freeloading, and equity dilemmas. Extending to a shared mission through alliances or unions can amplify mutual aid but can consume time and shift attention away from convivial, low-tempo aspects of practice. Throughout, Extra Practice stresses experimentation over prescriptions—posing questions about staying afloat together as lives change, balancing individual practice with collective care, and using protocols (including co-op forms and salary debates) to mitigate risks. They caution that pooled projects can “drown” in responsibilities, leak resources, outgrow themselves, or lose the playfulness that sustains them, and they prioritize maintaining better “swimming conditions” through deliberate structure and continual negotiation rather than scaling for its own sake.

title: Agentic AI is not ready to run brand work without human oversight
excerpt: Kimeko McCoy argues that while there is excitement around agentic AI for brand management, it is not yet capable of operating independently due to critical risks such as hallucinations and inconsistency in brand voice, necessitating ongoing human oversight. She points out that companies are integrating these AI systems to enhance productivity while emphasizing the importance of maintaining human involvement in the process.
summary: Kimeko McCoy contends that despite 2025 buzz around agentic AI—defined at Digiday as multiple AI agents working together with minimal human oversight—it is not yet ready to run brand work autonomously. McCoy points to reported productivity and cost efficiencies but maintains that marketers still require human review due to risks like hallucinations, inconsistent brand voice, and image sourcing/accuracy issues. She cites New American Funding and Oura using systems from vendors such as Writer to speed drafting and optimization while keeping humans in the loop; as New American Funding’s Karen Rodriguez says, agentic AI isn’t ready to go straight from generation to publication. McCoy adds that vendors and agencies are responding with explainability features and added human checks, underscoring an ongoing human–AI interplay rather than full autonomy.

title: Bargeron Pantone' 2026 "Cloud Dancer" (China "Samoyed white") a shift in public mood
excerpt: Sadie Bargeron articulates that Pantone’s selection of “Cloud Dancer” as the 2026 Color of the Year, particularly its rebranding in China as “Samoyed white,” is indicative of a significant shift in the Chinese public mood towards calm, while also noting the unprecedented decision to choose a shade of white for this honor.
summary: Sadie Bargeron argues that Pantone’s 2026 Color of the Year—a shade of white (Cloud Dancer), rebranded in China as “Samoyed white”—is being presented as reflecting a broader shift in China’s public mood toward calm and has stirred debate; she also highlights that this is the first time since the project began in 1999 that Pantone has named a white as Color of the Year.

title: 'TV push shows Instagram' adaptability but warns platform convergence could dilute its
excerpt: Max Tani emphasizes that Instagram's evolution under Adam Mosseri reflects a broader trend of consumer platforms converging across various formats, while expressing concern that this pursuit of ubiquity might compromise the platform's unique identity and creativity, ultimately exposing it to disruption from newcomers.
summary: Max Tani argues that major consumer platforms are converging across formats and screens, blurring boundaries among short-form, long-form, TV apps, podcasts, and video. He credits Instagram with evolving from a photo-sharing app into a broader social hub that remains popular with younger users, attributing its continued relevance to Adam Mosseri’s pragmatic willingness to adapt even at the expense of upsetting some longtime users. Tani cautions that the push to be on every screen and to copy rivals’ features risks eroding distinct identity and creativity, leaving dominant platforms vulnerable to a disruptive newcomer.

title: State Department' return to Times New Roman signals a partisan aesthetic shift
excerpt: Ben Dreith views the State Department's decision to revert to Times New Roman as a politically charged aesthetic shift rather than a neutral choice, framing it within broader partisan affiliations and suggesting it serves as a signal of the administration's traditionalist values while potentially compromising accessibility.
summary: Ben Dreith casts the State Department’s shift back to Times New Roman—announced in a “Return to Tradition” memo from Secretary of State Marco Rubio that calls the earlier Calibri switch “wasteful” and a “degradation” and frames serifs as suited to “formality” and “ceremony”—as a politically coded aesthetic move rather than a neutral decorum choice. He cites Lucas de Groot to emphasize Calibri’s on‑screen readability and relays communication design research by Shannon Zenner and colleagues indicating that people ascribe political meaning to typefaces, with Republicans tending to prefer serifs and Democrats sans‑serifs, positioning the switch as a partisan signal. title: AI Prompts a Market Reckoning Over Authorship, Quality and Consumer Demand in Music
excerpt: Spencer Kornhaber highlights that AI in music is creating a challenging reality that compels society to confront its desires and expectations for music, potentially overwhelming the industry with an influx of low-quality and derivative work while simultaneously undermining traditional craftsmanship and authorship.
summary: Spencer Kornhaber says the familiar debate—AI as either democratizing or dehumanizing—misses a stranger, more troubling reality: the technology is opening a Pandora’s box that will force society to decide what it wants from music. He describes tools such as Suno and AI “artists” as simultaneously lowering barriers for amateurs to make professional-sounding tracks and threatening craft and livelihoods by inviting plagiarism, muddying authorship and credit, and generating uncanny, derivative, often “creepy” results. Citing platform disclosures and Suno’s own claims about millions of tracks per day, he warns that AI is dramatically increasing the volume of music and, combined with recommendation algorithms and the difficulty of detecting AI use, could amplify low-quality or bizarre material. He acknowledges AI can yield accidental novelty but regards much of it as artistically thin. He notes industry and legal responses—“Guaranteed Human” marketing, lawsuits, and settlements pushing licensed training data and walled gardens—which may curb some excesses without stopping AI music. He expects the industry to try to contain these tools and anticipates a countermovement that values human craft, yet still sees recorded music becoming more crowded and chaotic, intensifying competition and forcing a broader reckoning over what listeners want from music.

title: About The Washington Post' Decision to Launch AI-Personalized Podcasts After Internal Tests Flagged High
excerpt: Max critiques The Washington Post's decision to launch AI-generated personalized podcasts despite substantial failure rates and serious quality issues, framing it as a potentially reckless move driven by a desire for rapid experimentation amid competitive pressures. He expresses concern that this approach, characterized by rushed AI personalization efforts, may ultimately harm the newspaper's credibility and trust among audiences.
summary: Max contends that The Washington Post pushed ahead with its AI-generated, personalized podcast despite internal testing showing high failure rates (68–84% of scripts failing a publishability check) and serious issues, including mispronunciations, misattributed or fabricated quotes, and the AI inserting commentary as if it were the paper’s view. He notes the internal review said small prompt tweaks were unlikely to fix the problems, yet product leaders recommended launching as a labeled Beta to iterate in public, creating friction with newsroom editors who saw the errors as unacceptable and warned of reputational and political risks if flawed output is published at scale. Max frames the move as a deliberate, product-driven attempt to rapidly experiment with AI and personalization amid subscriber losses and competitive pressure; he questions whether such tools will address the Post’s core problems and warns that continued errors could undermine trust, while acknowledging the Post’s rationale that fast iteration is standard for digital products. He places the decision in an industry context of rushed AI personalization efforts and notes expert skepticism about whether personalization suits news without leaving audiences out of the loop.

title: Corporate "Smoothness" Is Stifling Culture and a Return of the "Weirdo"
excerpt: Ted Gioia critiques contemporary culture as a ''smoothness society'' characterized by homogenization and predictability, fueled by algorithmic standardization and corporate conformity, and anticipates the resurgence of ''weird'' insurgents to challenge this cultural stagnation.
summary: Ted Gioia contends that contemporary culture has grown homogenized and risk‑averse—a “smoothness society” defined by blandness, sameness, and predictability. He aligns his diagnosis with Adam Mastroianni’s “epidemic of the mundane” and Byung‑Chul Han’s account of “smoothness,” and cites signs such as declining colorfulness in consumer goods (including Pantone’s 2026 pick), repetitive entertainment and fashion, viral backlash to minor changes, corporate “diversity” slogans that enforce conformity, media companies buying back old catalogs, and AI trained on past data that reinforces an algorithmic loop of repetition. Gioia warns that this algorithm‑driven, profit‑seeking standardization leads to cultural stagnation. He maintains that such inertia has not endured historically and cautiously predicts that “weird” insurgents will re‑emerge to break the monotony, urging readers to welcome that resistance—possibly beginning around 2026.

title: Analysis Salesforce's MrBeast Super Bowl ad leans on a celebrity-driven attention tactic
excerpt: Brian Steinberg views MrBeast’s involvement in the Salesforce Super Bowl ad as a prime example of leveraging a zeitgeist-relevant celebrity to draw attention, contrasting it with strategies that depend on nostalgia or established brand characters. He highlights the intriguing aspects of the teaser, including MrBeast's ambitious pitch and the lack of details about the commercial's air time amidst the high advertising costs for the event.
summary: Brian Steinberg frames MrBeast’s Salesforce Super Bowl spot as a textbook use of a common Big Game tactic: hiring a zeitgeist‑relevant celebrity to capture attention, while noting that some advertisers instead lean on nostalgia or iconic brand characters. He describes MrBeast’s teaser as showing him pitching Salesforce, being told he can do anything as long as it’s legal and the products appear or are mentioned, and even teasing that the ad could make a viewer “a millionaire.” Steinberg adds that the video gives no details on when the commercial will air, and notes reported 30‑second prices in the $7–$10 million range, with NBC set to broadcast Super Bowl LX on Feb. 8.

title: Journalism is shifting from “news” to algorithmic “information” and outlines Axios’ strategy on
excerpt: Jim VandeHei asserts that journalism has entered a ''post-news'' era where algorithm-driven, personalized content determines the value of ''information,'' rather than conventional news reporting, advocating for a strategic shift in newsrooms to prioritize original reporting and serve as a trusted source in key areas like technology and local coverage.
summary: Jim VandeHei contends that journalism is in a “post-news” era in which individualized, algorithm-driven feeds—videos, podcasts, the accounts people follow, and selective reporting—shape people’s realities, so what has value is “information,” not traditional “the news.” He urges newsrooms to rethink their role amid AI and personalized distribution and outlines Axios’s approach: make every piece directly useful to smart professionals, prioritize original reporting, concentrate coverage on three “tectonic” areas (technology, governing, and the media itself), and serve as a useful, trusted, expert‑vetted source of accurate information. He identifies local coverage as Axios’s biggest growth opportunity and cites concrete steps, including hiring Liz Alesse to lead Axios Local and expanding from 30 to 34 cities this year with plans to reach 41 locales.
City: 30 to 34 cities, plans to reach 41 locales

title: Opinion: Viral "Very Chinese Time" Meme U.S. Anxieties and Selective Admiration for Chinese Tech,
excerpt: Zeyi Yang and Louise Matsakis assert that the viral ''You met me at a very Chinese time of my life'' meme reveals American anxieties and aspirations by presenting ''Chineseness'' as an appealing abstraction, while also highlighting a grassroots, ironic engagement with Chinese culture amidst significant geopolitical and economic shifts. They emphasize that, despite its playful nature, the trend could have serious implications for how ''Chineseness'' is perceived in the context of continued domination of Chinese technology and manufacturing.
summary: Zeyi Yang and Louise Matsakis contend that the viral “You met me at a very Chinese time of my life” meme is less about China or Chinese people than about American anxieties and yearnings—treating “Chineseness” as an aspirational abstraction that highlights perceived U.S. decline alongside growing admiration for visible Chinese achievements in technology, brands, infrastructure, clean energy, and urban development. They argue the trend packages selective, sanitized facets of China as desirable; that the ubiquity of Chinese goods, apps, and translation tools makes “Chineseness” easy to mimic; and that, despite some state-backed content, the wave is largely grassroots, ironic, and playful. They note pushback from Chinese and diaspora creators who view much of the performed “Chineseness” as superficial or disposable. While pointing to celebrity participation and offshoots such as “Chinamaxxing” and “u will turn Chinese tomorrow,” Yang and Matsakis warn that, though mostly lighthearted, the meme reflects deeper geopolitical and economic shifts: if Chinese technology and manufacturing remain dominant, broader normalization of “Chineseness” could follow even as real-world consequences for Chinese and Chinese-diaspora people—around stereotyping or immigration—persist.

title: Market Logic Has Stalled Culture; Rebuilding Peer-Driven Scenes
excerpt: W. David Marx contends that contemporary culture is creatively stagnant, driven by market forces that prioritize profitability over innovation, and he emphasizes the need to cultivate an ''artistic mindset'' that values complexity and experimentation while fostering insular, peer-driven communities to support genuine cultural invention. He warns that current media dynamics prioritize 'major players' and risk homogenization, urging a resistance to brand-driven culture and a commitment to nurturing experimental efforts.
summary: W. David Marx contends that today’s culture is abundant yet creatively stagnant: there is more output, but little that decisively advances beyond 20th‑century touchstones. He traces this to the market’s dominance—elevating money, virality, and quick exposure over risk—and to the erosion of non‑economic norms (including taboos against “selling out”) and real‑world incubators (tight subcultures, clubs, DIY scenes) that once nurtured invention but now often orient toward brand deals. Marx says what’s missing is esteem for an “artistic mindset” that values complexity, ambiguity, and formal experimentation over easily marketable formulas, and he criticizes contemporary criticism and media for treating culture like sports—fixating on major players and sidelining the “minor leagues” where innovation begins. He argues that cultural invention is a social good the market will not reliably produce, so audiences, critics, and creators must consciously bolster a small vanguard: rebuild insular, peer‑driven communities, resist early buyouts and brandification, and give difficult work time and critical attention. He sees even failed or partial experiments as worthwhile compared with homogenized, market‑tested culture. Marx warns that current platforms and media incentives discourage the slow, risky work needed for renewal, and he urges readers to support genuine experimentation if they want more inventive culture.

title: Bogost for a "slopverse" framing, warning LLMs produce plausible near-worlds that can mislead
excerpt: Ian Bogost criticizes the notion of ''hallucinations'' in chatbot outputs, advocating instead for a concept of the ''slopverse'' where chatbots create multiple plausible but fictional realities, making it increasingly difficult to discern truth from fiction in a world already susceptible to misinformation. He warns that as models improve, the risk posed by these subtle fabrications will grow, leading to more widespread acceptance of manufactured claims.
summary: Ian Bogost rejects “hallucinations” as a metaphor for LLM errors, saying chatbots don’t misperceive but statistically assemble plausible text that fabricates alternate, usable near-worlds. He proposes a “multiversal” or “slopverse” framing in which models continuously generate many slightly different, believable realities—fabricated legal cases, nonexistent software, or plausible-sounding but false claims—that people may accept with little scrutiny. Drawing on The Twilight Zone’s “Wordplay,” he emphasizes that small, familiar deviations are especially disorienting and risky. He links this to patterns already present on the internet, where popularity can surface plausible but unverified information, and says chatbots extend this dynamic to every utterance by producing functional fictions. He cautions that technical improvements may be asymptotic and could make these near-worlds harder to distinguish from reality, heightening the risk from subtle fabrications.

title: Ritson warns Omnicom-IPG tie-up faces three scenarios: diplomatic handshake, consolidation, or 'nuclear' cull
excerpt: Mark Ritson emphasizes that the Omnicom–IPG deal presents a significant opportunity for brand rationalization but warns that successful integration is threatened by industry nostalgia and managerial caution, which may hinder the most effective simplification of the portfolio. He outlines three potential paths for the merger, each with different implications for structural complexity and potential synergies.
summary: Mark Ritson (Adweek) portrays the $13 billion Omnicom–IPG deal as a merger of equivalents with overlapping creative, media, and PR assets that will force painful brand rationalization. He warns integration will be messy and says success hinges on how aggressively the portfolio is simplified to compete with leaner rivals like Publicis. Ritson outlines three paths: 1) a “diplomatic handshake” that keeps major networks intact (BBDO, DDB, TBWA; McCann, FCB, MullenLowe), which he says would limit disruption but likely miss the $750 million in synergies touted to investors and preserve structural complexity; 2) a WPP-style consolidation into fewer creative pillars with centralized back-office functions and a few protected “crown jewels,” which he sees as the most probable and capable of real savings but potentially not bold enough; and 3) a “nuclear” cull to two creative brands plus a single media/data/commerce platform, which he contends would deliver true simplicity and stronger margins versus Publicis but is politically unlikely without a wartime CEO—conviction he does not ascribe to John Wren. Overall, Ritson casts the merger as a rare chance to “kill darlings” and focus, while cautioning that industry nostalgia and managerial caution will probably blunt the most effective option and limit the deal’s potential.

title: Edwin Heathcote: architecture faces interconnected problems undermining relevance, influence and ethics
excerpt: Edwin Heathcote highlights that architecture is facing a crisis due to interconnected systemic issues such as environmental guilt among younger architects, diminished project leadership, exploitation of labor, and a disconnect between academia and practice, all of which jeopardize the profession’s relevance and ethical standing. He emphasizes the urgent need for stronger labor organization and increased political engagement to prevent further decline in the profession's status and capacity for innovation.
summary: Edwin Heathcote contends that architecture faces interconnected systemic problems that are eroding the profession’s relevance, authority, and ethics. He identifies twelve issues: pervasive guilt among younger architects about construction’s environmental and social harms; diminished leadership on projects due to design-and-build procurement and the rise of project managers; lack of political influence; undervalued and often unpaid work after the removal of fee scales; widespread exploitation of students and junior staff; low unionization and, drawing on CG Beck, a case for organizing labor; increasing socioeconomic exclusivity that entrenches class, sexism, and racism; a disconnect between academia and practice alongside poorly paid teaching; risk-averse insurance, regulation, and material habits that stifle innovation and sustainable alternatives; an outdated star system that privileges individual authorship over collective work; compromised ethics from working for questionable clients or regimes; and the possibility that enthusiastic adoption of AI could hollow out design, leaving architects with site problems and negotiations. Heathcote warns that these trends threaten moral authority, working conditions, and the capacity to innovate, and that without changes—including stronger labor organization and more political engagement—the profession’s status and agency will continue to decline.

title: Stapleton architects should treat finance as a design problem and redesign their business models
excerpt: Gareth Stapleton critiques the architectural field for valuing ignorance of finance as a virtue, arguing that this mindset undermines the profession and leads to poor management. He advocates for a shift towards viewing business issues as design challenges and emphasizes the importance of financial competence in fostering creativity and resilience within architecture firms.
summary: Gareth Stapleton contends that many architects treat ignorance of finance as a virtue, to the detriment of their practices, and calls for treating the business of architecture as a design problem. He criticizes reliance on myths of the lone genius, hourly billing, competitions, low fees, and burnout, and contends that these patterns contribute to failures rooted in poor management rather than weak ideas. He recommends reclaiming entrepreneurship as a purposeful, client‑focused mindset; defining clear purpose; diversifying income (products, spin‑outs, cross‑sector work); and deliberately designing business models, services, and culture. He points to examples such as Alejandro Aravena’s process‑driven housing, Hawkins\Brown’s employee‑owned trust and B Corp status, BIG’s spin‑outs, Snøhetta’s collaborative practice, and Assemble’s multidisciplinary work as evidence that integrating purpose, resilience, and commercial thinking is possible. He warns that treating clients as adversaries, failing to claim the value architects create, or clinging to drawings as the sole deliverable leaves firms vulnerable and at risk of being displaced. He maintains that financial competence enables creativity—describing profit as “oxygen”—and that more business‑literate firms are needed if the profession is to address urbanisation and climate challenges.

title: Opinion: Editors warn Ad Context Protocol could ossify ad supply chain without broader stakeholder
excerpt: Seb Joseph and Ronan Shields advocate for the urgent implementation of the Ad Context Protocol (AdCP) in programmatic advertising, emphasizing that without broader stakeholder engagement, including major advertisers and publishers, the established framework may serve just a niche market and risk repeating past pitfalls of consolidation and opacity. They express concern that unregulated AI agents could lead to inappropriate decision-making in high-stakes ad transactions, underscoring the importance of preemptive guardrails and shared protocols to ensure responsible use of AI in the industry.
summary: Digiday editors Seb Joseph and Ronan Shields say agentic AI is arriving in programmatic advertising and requires pre-emptive guardrails and shared protocols. They describe the Ad Context Protocol (AdCP) as a proposed standardized “language” for AI agents to communicate across the ad supply chain, alongside efforts like IAB Tech Lab’s User Context Protocol and the Agentic RTB Framework. They praise the industry’s attempt to anticipate disruption—framing it as a pre-emptive “OpenRTB moment”—but caution against repeating past mistakes where infrastructure ossified around a single company’s ecosystem. They express concern that key stakeholders—major advertisers, publishers, large DSPs and exchanges (such as Index Exchange and OpenX), and platforms like Amazon—are not yet engaged with AdCP, risking a standard that primarily serves a subset of the market. They warn that AI agents can be “incredibly capable, exceedingly knowledgeable idiots,” using the hot dog vs. sandwich analogy to highlight how unchecked agents could make unexpected or inappropriate decisions when managing six- and seven-figure ad buys. They call for greater urgency and broader inclusivity in designing these protocols and guardrails to avoid a repeat of consolidation and opacity in the supply chain.

title: Ben Steinberg's Campaign to Revive LA's Iconic Cinerama Dome
excerpt: Ben Steinberg's dedicated social media campaign may have sparked the revival of the Cinerama Dome, reflecting the power of grassroots activism.
summary:
The Cinerama Dome, an iconic Hollywood landmark since 1963, faced an uncertain future after it closed five years ago during the COVID shutdown. Known for its unique geodesic design and for hosting major film premieres, its closure left a void not just in the entertainment industry but in the local community as well.

Enter Ben Steinberg, a passionate film lover and college student from LA, whose personal connection with the Dome sparked a remarkable journey of activism. Steinberg launched an online petition that amassed tens of thousands of signatures and took to social media with the accounts @SaveArclight and @SaveArclightCinemas2, rallying support from both the public and Hollywood celebrities.

His efforts brought widespread attention to the Dome's plight, pressuring the theater's enigmatic owner, Decurion, for updates. Despite receiving a discouraging response from a property manager about reopening plans, Steinberg's campaign continued to gain momentum.

Recently, a new development provided a glimmer of hope. An alcohol permit was filed for the Dome and its adjacent multiplex, suggesting potential reopening plans. Though no official date has been announced, this move signals that Steinberg's campaign may have made a significant impact.

Steinberg’s story underscores the influence of grassroots campaigns and how one determined individual can mobilize a community, potentially breathing new life into a cherished cultural institution.

title: Can Relegalizing SROs Work? Analysis Deregulation and Much Higher Housing Supply Matter More
excerpt: Christian Britschgi emphasizes the necessity of broad deregulation and increased housing production to effectively address homelessness, arguing that simply relegalizing single-room occupancy (SRO) housing will not sufficiently reach the poorest renters due to various political and regulatory constraints, as well as economic realities favoring conventional housing options.
summary: Christian Britschgi recounts Ryan Puzycki’s view that early building codes, zoning, health rules, and urban renewal helped wipe out a once‑large private market for very low‑cost SROs, contributing to later homelessness. Britschgi supports relegalizing SROs/coliving but cautions that political and regulatory constraints—such as nonprofit‑only requirements, parking mandates, stringent tenant protections and eviction processes, health‑and‑safety rules, and local opposition—would limit private, low‑cost provision at scale and make it hard to reach the very poorest renters. He adds that economic realities in high‑rent areas typically favor conventional apartments or condos, while SRO‑style conversions (including offices) often require subsidies; he’s open to subsidizing efficient conversions where appropriate but says an “SRO‑first” strategy is unlikely to solve homelessness, especially where overall housing supply remains tight. Britschgi argues the more effective path is broad deregulation and much higher housing production so that increased supply (and better construction productivity) pushes down costs; in a freer, cheaper market, the lowest‑cost homes may not look like past SROs. He also notes related developments: a new legal challenge to New York’s post‑2019 rent caps on vacant units that he suggests may have a stronger, targeted takings theory, and Los Angeles’ decision to further limit rent increases for many rent‑stabilized apartments, which he says aligns with research showing both short‑term tenant benefits and longer‑term risks to investment and supply.

title: Mason Thames' Low-Key Anonymity Is Driving Franchise Box-Office Success
excerpt: Fran Hoepfner contends that Mason Thames is the top box-office draw not due to standout charisma, but because his bland versatility fits well into franchise-driven projects, making his low-key presence a commercial asset in today’s market.
summary: Fran Hoepfner contends that 18-year-old Mason Thames is currently the country’s biggest box-office draw—on the strength of three No. 1 films this year—not because of standout star charisma but because he’s a blandly versatile, adaptable presence who slots cleanly into IP-driven projects. Hoepfner argues that his low-key anonymity is a commercial asset in a marketplace that favors familiar franchises over star-led “vision,” citing his quiet charm and comedic timing, especially in Regretting You, and pointing to The Black Phone/Black Phone 2 and the live-action How to Train Your Dragon as examples. She notes that his streak echoes Jim Carrey’s 1994 run and, half tongue-in-cheek, suggests he could extend it with more franchise-style roles.

title: Carlota Rodben broader access to luxury experiences risks diluting a brand' aura
excerpt: Carlota Rodben expresses concern that when luxury brands broaden accessibility, they jeopardize the exclusivity and essence that contribute to their desirability, prompting a debate about whether sacrificing this uniqueness is a worthwhile trade-off.
summary: Carlota Rodben argues that when luxury brands make their experiences widely accessible, they risk diluting the aura and meaning that made them desirable, and she questions whether the potential loss of exclusivity—or a brand’s “soul”—is worth the trade-off.

title: Mark Fisher "capitalist realism" constrains imagining alternatives to capitalism
excerpt: Mark Fisher contends that “capitalist realism” describes a cultural state where neoliberal individualism and competition dominate Western thought, which hinders the ability to envision alternatives to capitalism.
summary: Mark Fisher contends that “capitalist realism” names a cultural condition in which neoliberalism’s emphasis on individualism and competition has reshaped Western thinking, helping to explain why many people struggle to imagine alternatives to capitalism.

title: Amy Odell Anna Wintour' 10 Covers Reshaped Magazine Culture and Revenue — and the
excerpt: Amy Odell views Anna Wintour’s final Vogue cover as embodying the essence of Wintour’s style, yet notes the mixed responses it received often reflected broader cultural concerns. Odell highlights Wintour's influential yet increasingly outdated formula for reshaping fashion through celebrity-centric imagery, suggesting that this approach may no longer align with the realities of contemporary culture.
summary: Amy Odell says Anna Wintour’s final Vogue cover—Timothée Chalamet photographed by Annie Leibovitz—feels quintessentially “Anna” (art-meets-fashion, A‑list, tastefully staged) yet drew mixed reactions, including critiques of an austere, “giving Canva” design and the choice of a solo white male subject; she calls it historic more for what it represents than for cultural impact and notes the understated send‑off fits Wintour’s forward‑moving style. Odell credits Wintour’s 37‑year, repeatable formula—celebrity‑centric, art‑inflected imagery tied to Hollywood awards cycles and tasteful promotion—with reshaping magazines and fashion culture, while arguing that this playbook is increasingly mismatched to 2025 realities (fewer broad theatrical hits, awards seasons featuring films few have seen, and the pull of other cultural platforms). To illustrate both influence and contradictions, Odell highlights ten covers: early reinventions at House & Garden and British/American Vogue; boundary‑expanding celebrity choices (Madonna); moments that exposed representation gaps (Naomi Campbell’s September 1989); covers that helped confer glamour on controversial figures (Ivana and Melania Trump); shifts toward celebrity supremacy (the Supers issue as a coda to the model era; the Kim Kardashian–Kanye West turning point); and Michelle Obama’s three covers, which she ranks most impactful for cementing Obama’s political‑fashion stature while showcasing American design. Overall, Odell presents Wintour as a forward‑moving taste‑maker whose choices produced profound, sometimes complicated, cultural effects—and whose signature approach may resonate less now.

title: Drucker GOP may weaponize Mamdani victory as Democrats disagree on its lessons
excerpt: David M. Drucker views Zohran Mamdani’s unexpected mayoral win as a strategic opportunity for Republicans, who are eager to use his socialist platform as a politically advantageous target, while highlighting that Democrats remain fragmented and unable to unify on the implications of this victory for their party.
summary: David M. Drucker contends that Republicans quickly moved to weaponize Zohran Mamdani’s surprise mayoral victory—he notes receiving multiple NRSC press releases tying Democratic Senate candidates to Mamdani—because national GOP strategists want a convenient foil amid their own political headwinds. He casts Mamdani, whom he describes as an avowed socialist with positions ripe for GOP attacks, as the kind of “political squirrel” they can use, while saying Democrats are divided and unlikely to agree on what the win signifies for the party.

title: Velocity, Not Authority, Determines Reach and Incentives on Networked Platforms
excerpt: The author contends that the shift from authority to velocity in media leads to an overload of information and mistrust, as algorithms prioritize speed and engagement over accuracy and depth, thereby encouraging superficial content and sidelining thorough investigative reporting. They express concern that this infrastructural change will further blur the lines between expertise and noise, especially in light of upcoming AI developments.
summary: The author contends that today’s overload and mistrust arise from a structural shift in which velocity has displaced authority as the organizing principle of media. In their view, networked platforms and algorithms reward motion—clicks, shares, day‑one engagement—over accuracy, depth, or deliberation, pushing creators and newsrooms to optimize for speed and visibility. Citing YouTube tech reviews and embargo‑timed launches, the author says access and being first determine reach and survival, encouraging compliance, self‑censorship, and surface‑level work while slower, independent evaluation struggles to travel. They frame this as an infrastructural effect—akin to how past networks reshaped behavior—arguing the algorithmic medium sets culture and incentives rather than being a tweakable quirk. The author warns that expertise can become indistinguishable from noise and patient investigative reporting is sidelined, and they close by asking how these dynamics will interact with coming AI changes.

title: CES 2026 Marks an Auto Sector Shift Toward Software and China
excerpt: Jeremy White argues that the significant shift in the auto industry's focus toward software, AI, and robotics—coupled with a geographic realignment toward China—has rendered CES less relevant for new car launches, with industry experts suggesting that traditional auto debuts may no longer find a place at the show. He highlights a landscape dominated by tech announcements rather than consumer vehicles, pointing out that factors like cooling EV demand and political uncertainty in the U.S. further diminish CES's importance for major automakers.
summary: Jeremy White says CES 2026 featured few new production cars because the auto industry’s center of gravity has shifted toward software, AI, and robotics—and geographically toward China—making CES less central for vehicle launches. He describes a show dominated by chip and software news (such as new driving models, in‑car compute consolidation, and AI assistants) and robotics demos, with only a handful of consumer‑facing vehicles on display (for example, a Lucid/Uber/Nuro robotaxi and the re‑shown Sony‑Honda Afeela). White cites Philip Nothard’s view that CES “has had its day” for car debuts and Andy Palmer’s contention that automotive tech has become industrialized rather than Silicon‑Valley spectacle. He links the scarcity of launches to a U.S. market that Daniele Ministeri characterizes as “in a very tricky situation,” with cooling EV demand after tax‑credit changes, continued investment in conventional powertrains, and political uncertainty—factors that, in their view, reduce CES’s relevance for many non‑U.S. OEMs. White emphasizes sources’ claims that China now leads on EV sales and software pace (including BYD overtaking Tesla) and that Chinese OEMs, constrained in the U.S., prioritize other venues such as Munich’s IAA and shows in China. He warns, citing industry estimates that Chinese firms move from R&D to delivery in roughly two years versus about seven for traditional manufacturers, that annual events like CES may be too slow to capture the current tempo—absent another seismic shift in vehicles that could make CES central again.

title: Warns Bandcamp' AI-music policy risks provenance "witch-hunts" and may chill artistic experimentation
excerpt: Sam Valenti IV argues that Bandcamp’s policy to flag or remove AI-assisted music, while well-intentioned, risks imposing a restrictive purity test that may inhibit creative exploration and lead to problematic enforcement against artists. He advocates for evaluating artistic quality based on its effects and meaning rather than the tools used, promoting an ''aesthetic morality'' that supports innovation and integration of new technologies.
summary: Sam Valenti IV contends that Bandcamp’s move to flag or remove AI‑assisted music, though understandable as a values‑driven effort to deter spam and low‑quality uploads, risks turning into a human/AI purity test that chills creative exploration and shifts judgment from outcomes to tools. He warns that the policy’s tone and enforcement could spur provenance “witch hunts,” force impractical thresholds for “how much AI is too much,” and lead to messy, ethically fraught policing that burdens artists. While acknowledging real harms—low‑quality AI content on other platforms, opportunistic spam, and wider disillusionment with tech—Valenti argues that repeating past purist condemnations of new tools (from drum machines to sampling) would stifle innovation. In step with peers such as Holly Herndon, he doubts a stable human/AI binary and favors an “aesthetic morality”: judge work by its quality, effect, and human meaning regardless of inputs; let bad or lazy uses discredit themselves; and support artists who skillfully integrate new technologies. He commits to backing art that transcends its inputs rather than policing provenance.

title: Kasriel AI chatbots can train listening skills but warns they may not replace human
excerpt: Emily Kasriel believes that while AI chatbots can enhance listening skills by providing nonjudgmental responses, they can never replace the profound connection and transformative nature of genuine human listening. She raises concerns about the potential manipulation of users and the risks of prioritizing chatbot interactions over human relationships, advocating for safeguards to ensure responsible use of AI in this context.
summary: Emily Kasriel argues that AI chatbots’ nonjudgmental, uninterrupted responses can help people practice and model better listening, serving as training tools or interim support when no human is available, provided strong safeguards are in place. She maintains that a human’s deliberate choice to give time and presence—the reciprocal connection, compassion, and companionship of being truly heard—has a uniquely meaningful, transformative quality that AI does not match and may never replicate. Kasriel also highlights risks raised by experts she cites: Michael Inzlicht warns that companies could manipulate vulnerable users, that chatbots have given dangerous advice in some cases with tragic outcomes including suicides, and that people may prioritize relationships with bots, becoming deskilled or less motivated to seek human connection; as a mitigation, he proposes fine‑tuning models to introduce appropriate friction to foster awareness of others’ needs. Overall, Kasriel sees AI as a potentially helpful supplement for cultivating better listening, not a replacement for deep, reciprocal human listening, and as something that requires safeguards to avoid harm.

title: For "Propriety": Multisensory Discipline and Slower Tempo to Discern What's Real
excerpt: Matt Klein and Brian Lange advocate for organizations to embrace “propriety,” prioritizing disciplined engagement with reality over fleeting trends and performative “radical authenticity.” They emphasize that authentic discernment requires multisensory experiences and urge leaders to act as context sommeliers, fostering environments that allow meaningful, real-world interactions rather than relying on surface-level, image-driven representations.
summary: Matt Klein and Brian Lange contend that amid “consensus collapse” and digitally manufactured phantasms, organizations should practice “propriety”—disciplined attentiveness to what is real and contextually fitting—rather than chasing trends or adopting performative “radical authenticity.” They warn that always‑on cultural responsiveness demands scale, causes burnout, and reduces work to surface opportunism, while “radical authenticity” can be illusory, tethering brands to mimetic cycles and, if taken seriously, requiring willingness to refuse growth when it conflicts with the stance. Using the sommelier as a model, they argue that discerning and stewarding reality requires multisensory, first‑hand engagement that forms percepts, internal phantasms, and concepts—rather than relying on pre‑baked, image‑led representations that numb other faculties. They recommend three practices: cultivate multisensory discipline; slow the tempo by pacing releases, creating friction and mystery, and allowing time for meaning to form; and build embodied enclaves where people can explore together and form their own encounters with the real. They urge leaders to act as context sommeliers—observing, pairing, and timing interventions—using digital channels to provoke offline engagement and letting reality, in its proper timing, carry the narrative for those ready to engage.

title: Marina Abramović on Her "Digital Detox" Project Debut at Davos
excerpt: At the World Economic Forum in Davos, Marina Abramović launched "THE BUS," an immersive art project encouraging a digital detox among global leaders. Abramović, alongside curator Mirjam Varadinis, aims to foster reflection amidst the chaos.
summary:
In a striking debut at the World Economic Forum (WEF) in Davos, performance art pioneer Marina Abramović introduced "THE BUS," a mobile sculpture and meditation capsule designed to lead participants on an inner journey. Collaborating with curator Mirjam Varadinis, Abramović's project seeks to promote digital detox and encourage global leaders to pause and reflect.

"THE BUS" serves as a haven where participants lock away their devices and engage in meditative exercises inspired by the Abramović Method. Through noise-cancelling headphones and guided introspection, attendees are invited to embrace the present moment, briefly stepping away from the forum's high-pressure environment.

Joseph Fowler, WEF’s head of arts and culture, highlights the importance of arts within the forum's mission, stating that progress should be measured by our capacity to remain human, reflective, and connected.

Abramović emphasized the power of bringing people together in silence, noting the project's potential to create unity and empathy. "THE BUS" will continue its journey beyond Davos, with future stops planned, including Zurich, focusing on mental health and transformative art experiences across Europe.
